Limpopo Bridge Bus Crash

By: Kate Barry | Commission

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take a closer look at the Limpopo bridge where 44 pilgrims were killed on the Easter weekend. Was it a speeding bus driver, or did lack of maintenance contribute to the accident?

Unique Selling Point:
An interview with Road Safety Engineer Dr Louis Roodt, one of the experts who wrote the South African Road Restraint Systems Manual for the RTMC in 2022. He believes the damage to the temporary concrete barriers over the years has never been repaired. Although the height of 800mm meets the minimum safety requirements, they are not intact in places. The lack of maintenance by SANRAL is to blame for snagging the bus and flipping it over as it vaulted the bridge. Instead of possibly mitigating any damage, it made the accident much worse. Also, the fact that the outer steel barrier has been missing for a number of years offered no safety restraint and contributed to the loss of life.

Summary:
The tragic accident killed 44 pilgrims from Botswana on Maundy Thursday, as they travelled to the Easter celebrations at St Engenas ZCC in Moria. Only one 8-year-old girl miraculously survived. The Limpopo Transport MEC was quick to point out 'the human factor' as the reason for the crash. Back in Botswana the victims were given a State funeral and a mass burial - except for the 26-year-old bus driver who was ostracised in death and buried separately in his home village.
On closer inspection we expose the dire lack of maintenance on this extremely hazardous bit of road - a steep 3 km downhill and a sharp left-turn over the highest bridge in Limpopo. Google Streetview images show no maintenance of broken barriers in 2022 and 2023
SANRAL is responsible for this road, but a tender that was issued last year for Consulting Engineer Services for Routine Road Maintenance of the R518 was cancelled.
In 2018 photographs of a truck accident on the bridge show damage to the concrete barriers that was never repaired.
Video footage by passing motorists over the years also proves the point, as does drone footage shot by Elisha P Tungamirai 8 months ago. He writes: "Having personally visited the Mmamatlakala Bridge on the R518 on October 14th, 2023, I used my drone to capture the state of the barriers, particularly noting the dangerous terrain and the potential danger posed by a fall." Elisha just happens to be Structural Engineer specialising in bridges.
SANRAL is responsible for this road, but a tender that was issued last year for Consulting Engineer Services for Routine Road Maintenance of the R518 was cancelled in December.

Further information:
We potentially have an interview with the mother of 8-year-old Lauryn Siako, the sole survivor of the accident who was travelling with her Granny to Moria. While in Molepolole we would also film the gravesite of the victims and possibly speak to other families. This is the biggest loss of life in the history of Botswana road accidents and has greatly impacted this community.

Extra Budget Items:
Car rental and fuel to travel to the bridge in Limpopo
Flights to Gaborone
Car rental in Gaborone to travel the 57km to Molepolole
Possibly accommodation and S&T for one night, unless we can shoot everything in one day and fly home.
Possibly a fixer's fee to Botswana journalist in contact with the Siako family
3rd shoot day because of distances to travel

Script:


LIMPOPO BRIDGE

V/O: It’s Easter Sunday in Moria. Thousands of people have flocked to St Engenas ZCC church to celebrate its centenary.

For the first time since the pandemic, worshippers from across Southern Africa have made the pilgrimage to Limpopo. Even the President is here to congratulate Bishop Lekganyane, the leader of the Church.

Ramaphosa: I want to thank you for keeping yourselves healthy during the time of COVID-19.

V/O: But this celebration is shadowed by grief. Of the hundreds of buses that have made the journey, there is one that never reached the destination.

On Maundy Thursday, 45 pilgrims from Botswana were killed when their bus crashed over this bridge on the Mmamatlakala Pass and fell 24 metres into the ravine below.

Fire pic It was towing a trailer with gas bottles and stoves. When these burst into flames, the bus was burnt to ashes.

News: “An 8-year-old girl was the sole survivor of that devastating crash.”

V/O: Miraculously, Lauryn Siako was rescued by her granny Onkametse, before she herself succumbed to her injuries.
Within weeks the Presidents of both countries were at the bridge to inspect the scene.

President: But to have lost 45 people and souls is a sad moment for all of us.

V/O: But could this disaster have been averted? Our investigation suggests that negligence on the part of the road authority may have contributed to the carnage.

Fade to black

V/O: We travelled across the border to Molepolole, the largest village in Botswana. All 45 pilgrims on the bus came from this branch of the Zionist Christian Church.

Segometsi: The people that are very important at the church are all gone. The pastors they are four, they are all gone. There are only two left. There were six.

V/O: Segometsi David is a former secretary of the church, who lost several friends in the accident.

Segometsi: I was crying every time. Even now if I can imagine how they feel, how they…Hey, I’m starting to have a problem.

V/O: The bus driver was 28-year-old Ogaufi Noonyane who came from the neighbouring village of Thamaga. He was raised by his granny Kelebogile Moepywa.

Kelebogile: Ogaufi grew up as a child who was just respectful. He ended up saying he wants to be a driver. He never changed his mind.

Setshwano: He had been driving for some time, maybe about ten years or so.

V/O: Setshwano Mokgweetsinyana is Ogaufi’s uncle.

Setshwano: That Friday evening we saw some things on WhatsApp that a Botswana bus had crashed in South Africa. The terrible news were confirmed by the police.

Kelebogile: They just said the same bus that we heard has overturned with passengers in South Africa: Ogaufi Noonyane is one of those people. Then we were immediately filled with sorrow.

Setshwano: Ah…it brought a lot of pain.

V/O: This is the bus that Ogaufi drove that fateful weekend. A recently purchased 45-seater that collected the travellers from the Church in Molepolole.

Segometsi: We only use the route for Martin’s Drift. This is the route we use when we go to Moria. That one they have used; we don’t know it.

V/O: Instead of driving up to Martin’s Drift border post, and directly onto the N11, Ogaufi chose the closest crossing at Stockpoort Border Post. From there a complicated route led him onto the R518.

Link: So, this is the start of the pass. It’s steep, it’s straight and it continues like this for 3km. The speed limit is 60km/h and I constantly have to keep my foot on the brake just to slow down. If you didn’t know there’s a very sharp hairpin bend coming up, you’d be in trouble.
I’m constantly picking up speed. You still can’t even see the bridge yet. Look at this straight. So, there’s the turn, the hairpin bend; it’s quite straight I can pick up speed as well coming down here. Now it says 50km/h, the bumps in the road. Look how sharp this turn is.

Roodt: You look at the accident and where the bus ended, and the only conclusion is that there was excessive speed.

V/O: Dr Louis Roodt is a road safety expert who trains engineers to do road safety audits. He examined the circumstances around the bus accident and his findings are startling.

Roodt: If you come from the west side, downhill and a sharp curve, you can see most of the crashes happens where the vehicles just went straight. They could not negotiate that curve. The newly added concrete parapet wall was also damaged. Of that 30-odd metres, more than half is either gone or hanging over the side of the bridge.

Lourensa: And that was before the accident?

Roodt: Ja.

Link: Looking at these smashed concrete barriers, the twisted steel railing, the sheer drop-off where there’s absolutely no guard rail whatsoever: it’s easy to assume that the bus caused all this destruction.
But that is not the case. The truth is - this is what it looked like before the accident.

V/O: The Mmamatlakala bridge has a long history of accidents. In 2018 a truck and trailer lost its load of bricks on the bridge. The concrete barrier was damaged but never repaired, as this 2022 Google Streetview picture shows.

At a nearby filling station, cashier Petunia Makubela told us about another fatal accident on the bridge.

Petunia: There was a truck passing by with animals, yeah. It went off there and the driver died there. It was last year, I think.

V/O: In March 2023 a truck and trailer transporting game crashed over the bridge. The driver and his assistant were killed, along with 36 blesbok.

The damage from this accident wasn’t fixed either. Photos from July last year show even more destruction to the concrete barriers. This had a critical influence on the bus when it collided with the barrier at exactly the same point.

Roodt: The barrier was adequate, when it was new. It now has snag points. And you cannot say that it is functioning in the manner in which it was designed.

V/O: Having co-written the manual on South African Road Restraint Systems Dr Roodt knows a thing or two about how the barrier should function.

Roodt: It must contain the vehicle and typically the wheels will hit this solid object, turn and then skid. The car skids along the barrier.

V/O: This principle has been demonstrated in countless international crash tests. On colliding with the concrete barriers, the wheels of these heavy trucks and lorries are redirected onto the road, preventing the vehicles from overturning.
But that’s not what happened on the bridge.

Roodt: This barrier has been hit at several occasions, and these broken areas now present to the vehicle points on which it can catch. There’s a force that now withholds the vehicle, tries to break it. And in that process of not skidding along, but getting tangled and hooked, that acted like a tripping action and that is when the rolled over.

Lourensa: Are you saying then that if those sections were maintained, if the vehicle wasn’t able to be pulled or hooked as you are explaining it, this accident could have been prevented?

Roodt: That is my opinion, yes.

Link: So, who should have fixed these safety barriers? The management and maintenance of this road - the R518 – is the responsibility of SANRAL. Their routine patrols are meant to inspect all bridges on a weekly basis and to report on maintenance work that needs doing. So, how did they miss this?

SANRAL: Limpopo province falls under SANRAL’s Northern region. Surprisingly, they were well aware of the damaged barriers following a safety audit in February, a month before the bus crash.

Lourensa: But you accept that the bridge was quite damaged before the accident had taken place?

Progress: Yes, but it’s not anything that affects the safety of the bridge.

V/O: The Regional Manager Progress Hlahla is still waiting to receive the Accident Report.

Progress: From what we can see it has to do with some form of failure that the vehicle has suffered.

Lourensa: What would you say to someone who has expressed an expert opinion saying that the minute that the bus hit that barrier with the exposed rods, that it hooked onto the bus and forced the bus to flip?

Progress: Ah, that’s highly speculative. Then the barrier should have moved from its original position. There’s minor spalling of the rebar, but the containment system is intact.

Lourensa: If you’d seen the damage - and you have, because you’ve done the audit - why wasn’t the damage fixed?

Progress: So, I’m going to repeat again, now…

Lourensa: No, just give me a straight answer. Why wasn’t it? Was it too expensive?

Progress: No, the containment is adequate. There is nothing there that is urgent enough to fix it at that point because.

Lourensa: Well it isn’t, because forty-five people died.

Progress: Yes, but I would be very surprised if there’s an expert out there that comes to you to say the internal containment level is inadequate, and then speculate that because of that, then that’s why we had fatalities.

Lourensa: Well, we did speak to an expert who made that argument.

Progress: That would be very irresponsible for that expert, because…

Lourensa: So, you’re saying that’s wrong?

Progress: Ja, I’m disagreeing with it.

Roodt: Being in the condition that it is, with all these snag points, we cannot now say our noses are clean. A snagged and broken concrete barrier cannot be safe.

Link: The crash investigation report has yet to be released, and until then we can’t speculate on the findings. But we can pose the question: if the safety barriers had been properly maintained, if there was something here to stop the bus going over the edge, would so many lives have been lost?

V/O: In Molepolole Cemetery the 44 bus passengers are buried in a special section, forever united in death. They leave behind parents and children.
The driver, Ogaufi Noonyane is buried in his home town of Thamaga.

Setshwano: As a grandchild he was part of the support system of the family. He has a little son. By the time Ogaufi passed on, the child was about six months old.

V/O: The families of the deceased are able to claim from South Africa’s Road Accident Fund.

Klopper: If one of the deceased was a breadwinner then the loss of support is the claim that that family member will have.

V/O: Hennie Klopper is an Emeritus Professor of Public Law at the University of Pretoria.

Klopper: The average claim for loss of support is in the order of between R400 and R500 000 per dependent.

Lourensa: Is there a way to determine how many dependents those people might have had?

Klopper: According to South African statistics, you can take the average of dependency of about three persons per breadwinner.

V/O: But what about SANRAL’s liability? As a government agency, its constitutional duty is to ensure a safe travelling environment. But SANRAL believes the cause of the accident was speeding as opposed to any damage to the barrier, and is awaiting the Accident Report.

Lourensa: Do you think at the end of the day that they failed in their duty?

Roodt: Yes, because that is definitely over a long period. We shouldn’t have been put in a position where we must defend ourselves. We should have fixed the barrier.

Setshwano: It has shaken the country. It has shaken us all. And as the country moves on, like in the healing process, we hope in the end we will put this behind us and move on.

The newly added concrete parapet wall was also damaged. Of that 30-odd metres, more than half is either gone or hanging over the side of the bridge. Lourensa: And that was before the accident? Roodt: Ja. Link: Looking at these smashed concrete barriers, the twisted steel railing, the sheer drop-off where there’s absolutely no guard rail whatsoever: it’s easy to assume that the bus caused all this destruction. But that is not the case. The truth is - this is what it looked like before the accident. V/O: The Mmamatlakala bridge has a long history of accidents. In 2018 a truck and trailer lost its load of bricks on the bridge. The concrete barrier was damaged but never repaired, as this 2022 Google Streetview picture shows. At a nearby filling station, cashier Petunia Makubela told us about another fatal accident on the bridge. Petunia: There was a truck passing by with animals, yeah. It went off there and the driver died there. It was last year, I think. V/O: In March 2023 a truck and trailer transporting game crashed over the bridge. The driver and his assistant were killed, along with 36 blesbok. The damage from this accident wasn’t fixed either. Photos from July last year show even more destruction to the concrete barriers. This had a critical influence on the bus when it collided with the barrier at exactly the same point. Roodt: The barrier was adequate, when it was new. It now has snag points. And you cannot say that it is functioning in the manner in which it was designed. V/O: Having co-written the manual on South African Road Restraint Systems Dr Roodt knows a thing or two about how the barrier should function. Roodt: It must contain the vehicle and typically the wheels will hit this solid object, turn and then skid. The car skids along the barrier. V/O: This principle has been demonstrated in countless international crash tests. On colliding with the concrete barriers, the wheels of these heavy trucks and lorries are redirected onto the road, preventing the vehicles from overturning. But that’s not what happened on the bridge. Roodt: This barrier has been hit at several occasions, and these broken areas now present to the vehicle points on which it can catch. There’s a force that now withholds the vehicle, tries to break it. And in that process of not skidding along, but getting tangled and hooked, that acted like a tripping action and that is when the rolled over. Lourensa: Are you saying then that if those sections were maintained, if the vehicle wasn’t able to be pulled or hooked as you are explaining it, this accident could have been prevented? Roodt: That is my opinion, yes. Link: So, who should have fixed these safety barriers? The management and maintenance of this road - the R518 – is the responsibility of SANRAL. Their routine patrols are meant to inspect all bridges on a weekly basis and to report on maintenance work that needs doing. So, how did they miss this? SANRAL: Limpopo province falls under SANRAL’s Northern region. Surprisingly, they were well aware of the damaged barriers following a safety audit in February, a month before the bus crash. Lourensa: But you accept that the bridge was quite damaged before the accident had taken place? Progress: Yes, but it’s not anything that affects the safety of the bridge. V/O: The Regional Manager Progress Hlahla is still waiting to receive the Accident Report. Progress: From what we can see it has to do with some form of failure that the vehicle has suffered. Lourensa: What would you say to someone who has expressed an expert opinion saying that the minute that the bus hit that barrier with the exposed rods, that it hooked onto the bus and forced the bus to flip? Progress: Ah, that’s highly speculative. Then the barrier should have moved from its original position. There’s minor spalling of the rebar, but the containment system is intact. Lourensa: If you’d seen the damage - and you have, because you’ve done the audit - why wasn’t the damage fixed? Progress: So, I’m going to repeat again, now… Lourensa: No, just give me a straight answer. Why wasn’t it? Was it too expensive? Progress: No, the containment is adequate. There is nothing there that is urgent enough to fix it at that point because. Lourensa: Well it isn’t, because forty-five people died. Progress: Yes, but I would be very surprised if there’s an expert out there that comes to you to say the internal containment level is inadequate, and then speculate that because of that, then that’s why we had fatalities. Lourensa: Well, we did speak to an expert who made that argument. Progress: That would be very irresponsible for that expert, because… Lourensa: So, you’re saying that’s wrong? Progress: Ja, I’m disagreeing with it. Roodt: Being in the condition that it is, with all these snag points, we cannot now say our noses are clean. A snagged and broken concrete barrier cannot be safe. Link: The crash investigation report has yet to be released, and until then we can’t speculate on the findings. But we can pose the question: if the safety barriers had been properly maintained, if there was something here to stop the bus going over the edge, would so many lives have been lost? V/O: In Molepolole Cemetery the 44 bus passengers are buried in a special section, forever united in death. They leave behind parents and children. The driver, Ogaufi Noonyane is buried in his home town of Thamaga. Setshwano: As a grandchild he was part of the support system of the family. He has a little son. By the time Ogaufi passed on, the child was about six months old. V/O: The families of the deceased are able to claim from South Africa’s Road Accident Fund. Klopper: If one of the deceased was a breadwinner then the loss of support is the claim that that family member will have. V/O: Hennie Klopper is an Emeritus Professor of Public Law at the University of Pretoria. Klopper: The average claim for loss of support is in the order of between R400 and R500 000 per dependent. Lourensa: Is there a way to determine how many dependents those people might have had? Klopper: According to South African statistics, you can take the average of dependency of about three persons per breadwinner. V/O: But what about SANRAL’s liability? As a government agency, its constitutional duty is to ensure a safe travelling environment. But SANRAL believes the cause of the accident was speeding as opposed to any damage to the barrier, and is awaiting the Accident Report. Lourensa: Do you think at the end of the day that they failed in their duty? Roodt: Yes, because that is definitely over a long period. We shouldn’t have been put in a position where we must defend ourselves. We should have fixed the barrier. Setshwano: It has shaken the country. It has shaken us all. And as the country moves on, like in the healing process, we hope in the end we will put this behind us and move on.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We take a closer look at the Limpopo bridge where 44 pilgrims were killed on the Easter weekend. Was it a speeding bus driver, or did lack of maintenance contribute to the accident?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An interview with Road Safety Engineer Dr Louis Roodt, one of the experts who wrote the South African Road Restraint Systems Manual for the RTMC in 2022. He believes the damage to the temporary concrete barriers over the years has never been repaired. Although the height of 800mm meets the minimum safety requirements, they are not intact in places. The lack of maintenance by SANRAL is to blame for snagging the bus and flipping it over as it vaulted the bridge. Instead of possibly mitigating any damage, it made the accident much worse. Also, the fact that the outer steel barrier has been missing for a number of years offered no safety restraint and contributed to the loss of life.
metadata.Summary: The tragic accident killed 44 pilgrims from Botswana on Maundy Thursday, as they travelled to the Easter celebrations at St Engenas ZCC in Moria. Only one 8-year-old girl miraculously survived. The Limpopo Transport MEC was quick to point out 'the human factor' as the reason for the crash. Back in Botswana the victims were given a State funeral and a mass burial - except for the 26-year-old bus driver who was ostracised in death and buried separately in his home village. On closer inspection we expose the dire lack of maintenance on this extremely hazardous bit of road - a steep 3 km downhill and a sharp left-turn over the highest bridge in Limpopo. Google Streetview images show no maintenance of broken barriers in 2022 and 2023 SANRAL is responsible for this road, but a tender that was issued last year for Consulting Engineer Services for Routine Road Maintenance of the R518 was cancelled. In 2018 photographs of a truck accident on the bridge show damage to the concrete barriers that was never repaired. Video footage by passing motorists over the years also proves the point, as does drone footage shot by Elisha P Tungamirai 8 months ago. He writes: "Having personally visited the Mmamatlakala Bridge on the R518 on October 14th, 2023, I used my drone to capture the state of the barriers, particularly noting the dangerous terrain and the potential danger posed by a fall." Elisha just happens to be Structural Engineer specialising in bridges. SANRAL is responsible for this road, but a tender that was issued last year for Consulting Engineer Services for Routine Road Maintenance of the R518 was cancelled in December.
metadata.Further information: We potentially have an interview with the mother of 8-year-old Lauryn Siako, the sole survivor of the accident who was travelling with her Granny to Moria. While in Molepolole we would also film the gravesite of the victims and possibly speak to other families. This is the biggest loss of life in the history of Botswana road accidents and has greatly impacted this community.
